Review of Literature

Review of literature — purpose, sources, how to search, compile and write a literature review.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • Describe the purpose of a review of literature
  • List primary and secondary sources
  • Search a library and databases
  • Write a coherent literature review

In simple words

A review of literature is a careful study of what is already known about the problem. It prevents repetition, builds on prior work and helps to design the study.

Purposes

  • To know what is already known
  • To find the gaps and avoid repeating the study
  • To find a suitable tool and method
  • To place the study in context and justify it
  • To build a theoretical framework

Sources

Type Examples
Primary sources Research articles, theses, dissertations, conference papers
Secondary sources Textbooks, encyclopedias, reviews, indexes
Internet PubMed, CINAHL, Google Scholar, IRINS, national portals
Institutional INC and university libraries, WHO, ICMR journals

Database searching

  • Define the problem words, synonyms and keywords
  • Use Boolean operators: AND to narrow, OR to widen, NOT to exclude
  • Apply limits: years, language, study type, population
  • Retrieve the full text where possible

Compiling a literature review

  • Note author, year, place, sample, method, findings and limitations
  • Group studies by method or theme
  • Compare findings and note agreements and contradictions
  • Identify gaps and link them to the current study
  • Reference in an accepted style (APA or Vancouver) and avoid plagiarism

🔴 A review must show a gap, not a summary

The value of a review is a critical, reasoned statement of what is unknown and how the current study will answer it. Simply listing studies is not a review.

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. Review of literature finds what is known and what is missing.
  2. Primary sources are original research; secondary sources summarize it.
  3. Use Boolean operators and limits for an efficient search.
  4. Record author, year, sample, method and findings for each study.
  5. A review must show the research gap.

⭐ Important for exams

  1. Plagiarism is avoided by citing all sources.
  2. Prefer recent studies of good quality.
  3. A matrix table makes comparisons easier.
  4. Theoretical framework grows out of the review.
  5. Reference styles: APA and Vancouver.

📌 Memory trick

Search: W-W-S-L — Words, Widen or Narrow (AND, OR), Select, Limit.

60-second revision

  • Review finds known, unknown and gaps.
  • Primary versus secondary sources.
  • Boolean operators and database limits.
  • Record and compile into themes.
  • Write critically; cite correctly; end at the gap.

Test yourself

A primary source in research is:

Answer: B. Primary sources report original research findings directly.

Using AND in a database search:

Answer: B. AND narrows the search by requiring both terms to appear.

The final part of a literature review states:

Answer: B. The review must end with the gap that the present study will address.

Which is recorded for each study reviewed?

Answer: B. Each study is summarised by sample, method, findings and limitations for comparison.

Plagiarism is avoided by:

Answer: B. Proper citation of all sources, ideas and figures avoids plagiarism.
